added_claims.speaker: opening speaker (Graham founder, introducing the panel)
added_claims.quote: as I look back over the last decade as I said earlier it was absolutely phenomenal for beta as I look ahead I'm not so sure how constructive it is for traditional Investments
added_claims.claim: The past decade rewarded passive stock and bond beta, but the coming years look much less constructive for traditional investments and better for macro because volatility is expected across FX, rates, equities and commodities.
added_claims.direction: traditional beta returns lower; macro opportunity higher
added_claims.testable: partly - compare 60/40 vs macro index returns across inflation regimes

added_claims.speaker: Chris McCann
added_claims.quote: when we're doing asset allocation every month we're trying to make sure that we're taking pairwise correlation into account so that we're not putting all of our assets into one style of investing
added_claims.claim: Capital is allocated across portfolio managers monthly using their pairwise return correlations, and PMs are hired for what they add that is different, so the book is not concentrated in one style.
added_claims.testable: yes - diversification ratio of correlation-aware vs naive allocation

added_claims.speaker: David Keelan
added_claims.quote: at what point can they really step in and intervene in the currency if they're um you know buying all the treasuries or all the jgbs
added_claims.claim: Japan's yield-curve control (buying large amounts of JGBs) conflicts with intervening to support the yen, so with inflation at a 30-year high and markets testing YCC, the policy mix looks unsustainable and is a trade opportunity.
added_claims.indicator: BoJ yield-curve control, JGB purchases, USDJPY intervention
added_claims.conditions: Japanese inflation rising while YCC holds
added_claims.testable: partly - yen and JGB moves around intervention and YCC changes

added_claims.speaker: David Keelan
added_claims.quote: the central banks going probably a little farther than the market
added_claims.claim: View: central banks will tighten somewhat further than market pricing implies because inflation is sticky.
added_claims.testable: yes - realised vs priced terminal rate

added_claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
added_claims.quote: for me it's bottom up so I try to find ideas um and once so the ideas come together and I look at my overall risk and make sure it's oriented to um the way we want it
added_claims.claim: Portfolio construction method: generate trade ideas bottom-up, then check the combined book's overall risk orientation, using the same process in quiet (2018) and busy (2022) years.

added_claims.speaker: David Keelan
added_claims.quote: if you write it it works you feel it it's at the portfolio level but you don't want to be too big that if there's some noise you get shaken out
added_claims.claim: Sizing rule: a position should be big enough to matter at the portfolio level if right, but small enough that ordinary noise does not force you out; getting the theme right matters more than structure.
added_claims.testable: partly - stop-out frequency vs position size in volatility units

corrections.issue: Speaker frames dire sentiment and the risk of a snapback as an opportunity to trade, not only a risk for a trend short; 'trend-following' was not said.
corrections.fix: Bear markets contain vicious rallies (summer 2022: stocks +20%, 10-year notes rallying 75bp, stock-bond rallying together), and recognising when sentiment is so dire that the market can snap back is itself the trading opportunity.

corrections.issue: The Mexican peso appreciated while also paying high carry (reshoring), not 'despite carry'.
corrections.fix: Most 2022 returns came from short stocks plus short bonds (anti-risk-parity) and long dollar, with further gains in yen moves and the Mexican peso, which appreciated on top of its large carry on reshoring to North America.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker for most of the claim: Peter Chapson only said it defies imagination that Japan alone avoids inflation; the 30-year-high CPI, YCC testing, weak yen, intervention and BoJ leadership points are David Keelan's.
corrections.fix: Peter Chapson: it is implausible that Japan stays the only developed country without inflation, and people stuck in old ways miss this. David Keelan: Japan's 3% CPI (30-year high), markets testing YCC, the weak yen, intervention limits and the coming BoJ leadership change make Japan a key opportunity.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: the first answer (vol-unit sizing, liquidity, bottom-up, 'as Dave mentioned earlier') is Peter Chapson's.
corrections.fix: Peter Chapson: size positions in volatility units so higher volatility means smaller positions; prepare for tails and gap risk.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: this is Peter Chapson's answer (he refers to 'Dave' in the third person).
corrections.fix: Peter Chapson: poor market liquidity means some trades cannot be sized large enough to matter, so they are skipped; place a premium on liquid instruments.

completeness_estimate: 0.86 - first reader covered nearly all mechanisms and risk methods; missed the beta outlook, PM allocation by pairwise correlation, BoJ YCC-vs-intervention conflict, sizing-vs-noise rule and bottom-up process; several speaker attributions in C07-C09 were wrong
